messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus was thirty-three years old, a prosecutor in a major city, when the bomb went off in the federal plaza. He had been walking back from a coffee shop, the morning still quiet, when the air turned inside out. What he remembered best was not the blast itself but the seconds after: the ringing silence, the dust falling like snow, a woman’s shoe lying on its side a few feet away. He had crouched behind a concrete planter, and later, when the paramedics came, he had helped them carry a man whose leg was wrong. He could not tell a clear story of what happened, even to himself. The pieces were there—the shoe, the dust, the man’s weight—but they did not arrange themselves into a narrative. They hung in his mind like photographs without captions, more real than any ordinary memory, so vivid that sometimes, walking into his office, he would feel the grit of concrete on his palms and know, with absolute certainty, that it was happening right now.

In the months that followed, Marcus returned to work. The courthouse was three blocks from the plaza, and he passed the barricades every morning without looking at them. What he could not avoid was the smell of alcohol. A colleague came back from lunch one day, and the faint sweetness on his breath hit Marcus like a wall. He felt his chest lock. The colleague had been drinking—just a beer, he said later—but in that moment Marcus was certain that he should have known, should have stopped it. He had not done enough. He had not protected anyone. The guilt was a weight he carried into every room: he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, even though he knew, rationally, that there was nothing he could have done. The feeling did not listen to reason.

The memory looped back on itself. The more he told himself he had failed, the more the memory of the plaza came alive—the shoe, the dust, the man’s leg—and the more alive it felt, the more certain he became that he should have acted. He began to distrust people in a way he had not before. A witness in a trial gave him a straightforward account, and Marcus found himself searching for the lie, the hidden thing. People are not what they seem, he thought, and the thought felt like a law of physics. It made him vigilant. He started scanning rooms for exits, for the shape of a bag that did not belong, for the smell of alcohol on someone’s breath at a dinner party. The fatigue that followed was bone-deep. He would come home exhausted, his wife already asleep, and lie awake with the memory pressing in.

The causal connections tightened into a cycle he could not name. A loud bang—a car backfiring on the street outside his office—would send him back to the plaza, and from there the guilt would rise, and then the distrust, and then the scanning, and then the exhaustion, and then the next bang would feel inevitable. He stopped going to restaurants with bars. He stopped taking the subway. He told his wife he was fine, but she had started sleeping in the guest room, and he knew she was tired of his silences.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in court. He had been cross-examining a witness when the air conditioning unit clanked, a sound like a metal door slamming. Marcus froze. The judge asked if he was all right. He said yes, but he could not remember the next question. That night, sitting in his car outside his house, he understood that he was afraid of his own mind—afraid that the memory would never stop feeling like the present, and that he would lose everything he had not already lost.
